Noise-regularized training of quantum circuit Born machines under a finite shot budget

Hoang M. Ngo Email: hoang.ngo@ufl.edu Affiliation: Department of Computer and Information Science and Engineering, University of Florida, 1889 Museum Road, Gainesville, 32611, Florida, USA    Quan Nguyen Email: quan.nguyen1@ufl.edu Affiliation: Department of Computer and Information Science and Engineering, University of Florida, 1889 Museum Road, Gainesville, 32611, Florida, USA    Jung Taek Seo Email: seojt@gachon.ac.kr Affiliation: Department of Smart Security, Gachon University, 1342 Seongnam-daero, Sujeong-gu, Seongnam-si, 13120, Gyeonggi-do, Republic of Korea    Wanli Xing Email: wxx151@miami.edu Affiliation: Department of Teaching and Learning, School of Education and Human Development, University of Miami, 5202 University Drive, Coral Gables, 33124, Florida, USA    My T. Thai Email: mythai@cise.ufl.edu Affiliation: Department of Computer and Information Science and Engineering, University of Florida, 1889 Museum Road, Gainesville, 32611, Florida, USA
Abstract

Quantum circuit Born machines (QCBMs) can learn distributions that are hard to sample from classically, but their value depends on generalizing from finite training data. Here, we study how hardware noise affects this generalization. We show that, for any noise process, the generalization gap of a QCBM trained with the maximum mean discrepancy is bounded by the complexity of the distributions the noisy model can reach. Scrambled local Pauli noise contracts this complexity but biases the model towards the uniform distribution, so residual noise acts as a regularizer whose optimal strength can be intermediate. We propose GENIE, a framework that realizes a chosen noise level with capped error mitigation and selects it during training from held-out data within a fixed execution budget, with provably bounded regret. In simulations on synthetic and census data, GENIE stays close to the best of four noise-control strategies, whereas every fixed noise level falls short in many settings.

keywords
quantum computing, generative model, error mitigation

1 Introduction

Generative modelling, the task of learning an unknown probability distribution from examples and producing new samples from it, is one of the most natural tasks for a quantum computer. The reason is measuring a quantum state already yields a sample from a probability distribution Perdomo-Ortiz et al. (2018). Parameterized quantum circuits can prepare output distributions that are believed to be hard to sample from classically Bremner et al. (2016); Arute and others (2019); Coyle et al. (2020), and quantum generative models admit provable expressivity and learnability separations from classical models Gao et al. (2018); Gao et al. (2022); Sweke et al. (2021). The most direct realization of this idea is the quantum circuit Born machine (QCBM) Benedetti et al. (2019); Liu and Wang (2018), whose model distribution is given by the Born rule, q𝜽​(𝒙)=|⟨𝒙|U⁡(𝜽)|𝟎⟩|2q_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x})=|\langle\boldsymbol{x}|U(\boldsymbol{\theta})|\boldsymbol{0}\rangle|^{2}, for a parameterized circuit U⁡(𝜽)U(\boldsymbol{\theta}). Every circuit execution thus returns an exact sample, and because only samples rather than likelihoods are accessible, QCBMs are trained with sample-based losses such as the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) Gretton et al. (2012); Liu and Wang (2018); Rudolph et al. (2024). QCBMs have been demonstrated on trapped-ion hardware Rudolph and others (2022), high-energy physics Kiss et al. (2022), combinatorial optimization Alcazar et al. (2024) and drug discovery Ghazi Vakili et al. (2025).

To be practically useful, a Born machine must generalize beyond its training set rather than reproduce it. For a generative model, generalization is defined as the closeness of its output distribution to the unknown target distribution pp, rather than to the empirical distribution of the mm training samples. Operationally, it is the ability to produce valid samples that never appeared in training Gili et al. (2024). For a sufficiently expressive model, driving the training loss to zero instead reproduces the empirical distribution, which places all of its mass on the observed bitstrings and none on valid but unseen ones Rudolph et al. (2024). This is the generative form of overfitting, and Born machines are particularly exposed to it. Specifically, their output space contains 2n2^{n} bitstrings while practical training sets are only polynomially large, so the empirical distribution leaves almost every valid bitstring unobserved. Generalization bounds and regularizers developed for supervised quantum learning Abbas et al. (2021); Banchi et al. (2021); Caro et al. (2022); Du et al. (2022b); Kobayashi et al. (2022) do not transfer directly, because they act on a predictor that maps inputs to labels, whereas a Born machine has neither and outputs only the distribution it samples. Recent studies have begun to examine generalization in Born machines by bounding the excess MMD risk of an idealized empirical minimizer Du et al. (2022a), benchmarking the validity, novelty and coverage of generated samples Gili et al. (2023); Gili et al. (2024), and showing that a converged MMD is an unreliable indicator of generalization Raj et al. (2026). However, these works evaluate generalization rather than control it, and they offer no mechanism for regularizing the finite-shot, noisy training that Born machines undergo on real hardware.

In classical learning, injecting stochasticity into training is a common way to improve generalization, whether through input noise Bishop (1995), dropout Srivastava et al. (2014) or stochastic gradient descent Hardt et al. (2016). Quantum hardware provides such stochasticity intrinsically from gate errors and decoherence. In supervised quantum learning, analyses Bu et al. (2023); Du et al. (2022b); Khanal and Rivas (2025) show that it can act as an implicit regularizer Heyraud et al. (2022), with a finite optimal noise level that can be targeted by tuning the noise Zhang et al. (2026); Kuzmin et al. (2025); Scala et al. (2026), although excessive noise destroys trainability Wang et al. (2021). For Born machines, exploiting this noise is more challenging. The noisy output distribution is itself the model, so the noise that suppresses overfitting also distorts what is learned. Moreover, the noise level is fixed by the hardware, and lowering it requires error mitigation whose sampling cost grows exponentially with the amount of noise removed Temme et al. (2017); Mari et al. (2021); Takagi et al. (2022); Quek et al. (2024). To build a noise-based regularizer for QCBMs, we must therefore answer two questions: (i) how does residual hardware noise affect the generalization of an MMD-trained Born machine? (ii) how can the amount of residual noise be selected and realized during training within a finite budget of circuit executions?

In this work, we answer these questions and develop GENIE (generalization with inherent noise), a framework that treats residual hardware noise as a tunable regularizer for MMD-trained Born machines (Fig. 1). Our contributions are as follows.

  • •

    Generalization theory. We derive a bound on the empirical-to-population MMD gap of QCBMs that holds for any noise process and training algorithm. In addition, we specialize it to scrambled local Pauli noise, where residual noise contracts the gap by the retained-signal factor 1−γ1-\gamma. The bound makes the regularization effect of residual noise explicit, while showing that the same noise biases the model towards the uniform distribution, so the amount of noise to retain must be chosen.

  • •

    Adaptive noise regularization. We propose GENIE, a framework that adaptively selects the residual noise for MMD-trained QCBMs under a fixed circuit-execution budget. In general, first it realizes each level with capped probabilistic error reduction, which removes just enough hardware noise while keeping the remaining noise close to white noise. Then, it periodically spends a small portion of the budget to probe candidate noise levels on held-out data, and then selects the level for the next training block based on validation performance and the budget remaining for training. We establish a cumulative selection regret bound that quantifies how limited validation data, measurement precision, and the frequency of noise adjustments affect the controller’s decisions along the training trajectory.

  • •

    Empirical validation. We compare GENIE with training at three fixed noise levels, namely no, half and full mitigation, under matched budgets of circuit executions. In simulations on three synthetic datasets with 1212 qubits, it is within 1%1\% of the best of the four methods in 64%64\% of 144144 conditions and has a median regret of 0.3%0.3\%, whereas the fixed levels have median regrets between 8.4%8.4\% and 22.7%22.7\%. On the Adult census dataset with 1010 qubits at strong noise, it gives the most accurate population shares, income rates within groups and income predictions of the four methods.

2 Results

2.1 Preliminaries

This subsection introduces the model, the noise and the loss, and the two quantities in which all of our results are stated, which are, the witness function and the Rademacher complexity.

Born machines under hardware noise.

Let 𝒳={0,1}n\mathcal{X}=\{0,1\}^{n} be the set of nn-bit strings. A Born machine applies a parameterized circuit U⁡(θ)U(\theta), θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta, to a fixed input state ρ0\rho_{0}, typically |0⟩⊗n\ket{0}^{\otimes n}, and measures all qubits in the computational basis. By the Born rule, its ideal output distribution is

qθ0​(x)=⟨x|​U​(θ)​ρ0​U​(θ)†​|x⟩,x∈𝒳.q_{\theta}^{0}(x)=\bra{x}U(\theta)\rho_{0}U(\theta)^{\dagger}\ket{x},\qquad x\in\mathcal{X}. (1)

On hardware, the circuit runs under a noise process 𝒩\mathcal{N}, which may include gate errors, correlated errors and readout errors. If ρθ𝒩\rho_{\theta}^{\mathcal{N}} denotes the resulting output state, each circuit execution returns one sample from the noisy distribution

qθ𝒩​(x)=⟨x|​ρθ𝒩​|x⟩.q_{\theta}^{\mathcal{N}}(x)=\bra{x}\rho_{\theta}^{\mathcal{N}}\ket{x}. (2)

The probabilities qθ𝒩​(x)q_{\theta}^{\mathcal{N}}(x) are never observed, only samples from them. Therefore, the Born machine is an implicit generative model, and the distribution that is trained and evaluated is the noisy qθ𝒩q_{\theta}^{\mathcal{N}}, not the ideal qθ0q_{\theta}^{0}.

To model the noise, we use the standard model of local gate noise. Each of the ss two-qubit gates in the circuit is followed by an independent stochastic Pauli channel on each of the two qubits it acts on. Indexing these L=2​sL=2s noisy locations by kk, the channel at location kk is

ℰk​(ρ)=(1−ϵk)​ρ+ϵk​∑P∈{X,Y,Z}πk​(P)​P​ρ​P,∑Pπk​(P)=1,\mathcal{E}_{k}(\rho)=(1-\epsilon_{k})\rho+\epsilon_{k}\sum_{P\in\{X,Y,Z\}}\pi_{k}(P)\,P\rho P,\qquad\sum_{P}\pi_{k}(P)=1, (3)

with probability ϵk\epsilon_{k} an error occurs, and the error is a Pauli PP drawn from the distribution πk\pi_{k}. Randomized compiling brings general gate noise into this form, after which the error rates can be measured Wallman and Emerson (2016); van den Berg et al. (2023). We call ϵ=(ϵ1,…,ϵL)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}=(\epsilon_{1},\ldots,\epsilon_{L}) the hardware noise profile. It is fixed by the device, and later we reduce it selectively to a residual profile 𝐫\mathbf{r} with 0≤rk≤ϵk0\leq r_{k}\leq\epsilon_{k}.

Learning problem and MMD loss.

The target distribution pp on 𝒳\mathcal{X} is unknown and is accessible only through a training sample 𝒮=(x1,…,xm)\mathcal{S}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}) of mm independent draws from pp. The goal is a model whose distribution is close to pp itself, not merely to the mm observed strings. Because only samples of the model are available, we measure closeness with a kernel κ:𝒳×𝒳→[0,1]\kappa:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\to[0,1] between bit strings that is positive semidefinite and satisfies κ⁡(x,x)=1\kappa(x,x)=1. A standard choice for Born machines is the Gaussian kernel on the Hamming distance dHd_{H}, κ(x,y)=1c∑i=1cexp[−dH(x,y)/(2τi2)]\kappa(x,y)=\frac{1}{c}\sum_{i=1}^{c}\exp[-d_{H}(x,y)/(2\tau_{i}^{2})], with bandwidths τ1,…,τc\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{c} Liu and Wang (2018); Rudolph et al. (2024). The kernel defines a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) ℋ\mathcal{H} of functions on 𝒳\mathcal{X}, in which κ⁡(x,⋅)\kappa(x,\cdot) serves as a feature vector of the string xx, with ⟨κ⁡(x,⋅),κ⁡(y,⋅)⟩ℋ=κ⁡(x,y)\left\langle\kappa(x,\cdot),\kappa(y,\cdot)\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\kappa(x,y). Averaging these features over a distribution ν\nu gives its kernel mean embedding, and the distance between two embeddings is the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) Gretton et al. (2012):

μν:=𝔼x∼ν​[κ⁡(x,⋅)]∈ℋ,MMDκ​(ν,ν′):=‖μν−μν′‖ℋ.\mu_{\nu}:=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\nu}\bigl[\kappa(x,\cdot)\bigr]\in\mathcal{H},\qquad\mathrm{MMD}_{\kappa}(\nu,\nu^{\prime}):=\left\lVert\mu_{\nu}-\mu_{\nu^{\prime}}\right\rVert_{\mathcal{H}}. (4)

The population risk of the noisy model is its squared MMD to the target,

R𝒩​(θ):=MMDκ2​(qθ𝒩,p)=𝔼y,y′∼qθ𝒩​[κ⁡(y,y′)]⏟model–model+𝔼x,x′∼p​[κ⁡(x,x′)]⏟target–target−2​𝔼x∼p,y∼qθ𝒩​[κ​(x,y)]⏟coupling,R_{\mathcal{N}}(\theta):=\mathrm{MMD}_{\kappa}^{2}\bigl(q_{\theta}^{\mathcal{N}},p\bigr)=\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{y,y^{\prime}\sim q_{\theta}^{\mathcal{N}}}\bigl[\kappa(y,y^{\prime})\bigr]}_{\text{model--model}}+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{x,x^{\prime}\sim p}\bigl[\kappa(x,x^{\prime})\bigr]}_{\text{target--target}}-2\,\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p,\,y\sim q_{\theta}^{\mathcal{N}}}\bigl[\kappa(x,y)\bigr]}_{\text{coupling}}, (5)

where all draws are independent. The coupling term rewards model samples that resemble the data, the model–model term penalizes a model whose samples all resemble each other, and the target–target term is a constant.

Training, evaluation and the generalization gap.

A learning algorithm 𝒜𝒩\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{N}} maps the training sample to parameters θ^𝒩=𝒜𝒩​(𝒮)\hat{\theta}_{\mathcal{N}}=\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{N}}(\mathcal{S}). It may be randomized, for example through the initialization, stochastic optimization and the finite number of shots used in training. Because pp is unknown, the risk of the learned model can only be estimated. To do so, we draw NN fresh samples 𝒴=(y1,…,yN)\mathcal{Y}=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{N}) from the learned circuit, independent of 𝒮\mathcal{S} and of the training randomness given θ^𝒩\hat{\theta}_{\mathcal{N}}, and replace each expectation in equation (5) by an average over distinct pairs:

R^𝒮,𝒴𝒩​(θ):=1m⁡(m−1)​∑i≠i′κ⁡(xi,xi′)+1N⁡(N−1)​∑j≠j′κ⁡(yj,yj′)\displaystyle\widehat{R}^{\mathcal{N}}_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{Y}}(\theta):=\frac{1}{m(m-1)}\sum_{i\neq i^{\prime}}\kappa(x_{i},x_{i^{\prime}})+\frac{1}{N(N-1)}\sum_{j\neq j^{\prime}}\kappa(y_{j},y_{j^{\prime}}) −2m​N∑i=1m∑j=1Nκ(xi,yj),\displaystyle-\frac{2}{mN}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\kappa(x_{i},y_{j}), (6)
m,N≥2.\displaystyle\qquad m,N\geq 2.

For a fixed θ\theta, this U-statistic is an unbiased estimate of R𝒩​(θ)R_{\mathcal{N}}(\theta). For the learned parameters it is not, because θ^𝒩\hat{\theta}_{\mathcal{N}} was chosen using the same training strings that appear in the estimate. The generalization gap measures the resulting optimism,

Δ𝒩​(m):=𝔼𝒮,𝒜𝒩,𝒴​[R𝒩​(θ^𝒩)−R^𝒮,𝒴𝒩​(θ^𝒩)].\Delta_{\mathcal{N}}(m):=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{N}},\mathcal{Y}}\Bigl[R_{\mathcal{N}}(\hat{\theta}_{\mathcal{N}})-\widehat{R}^{\mathcal{N}}_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{Y}}(\hat{\theta}_{\mathcal{N}})\Bigr]. (7)

Therefore, a low empirical risk certifies a low population risk only if the gap is small. For example, a model that simply reproduces the empirical distribution p^m\hat{p}_{m} of the training strings has an empirical risk of at most zero on average over 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, although its population risk MMDκ2​(p^m,p)\mathrm{MMD}^{2}_{\kappa}(\hat{p}_{m},p) is positive whenever p^m≠p\hat{p}_{m}\neq p.

Witness functions.

Only the coupling term in equation (5) involves both the model and the data. It is described by the witness function of a generator,

hθ𝒩​(x):=⟨μqθ𝒩,κ⁡(x,⋅)⟩ℋ=𝔼y∼qθ𝒩​[κ⁡(x,y)]∈[0,1],h_{\theta}^{\mathcal{N}}(x):=\left\langle\mu_{q_{\theta}^{\mathcal{N}}},\kappa(x,\cdot)\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim q_{\theta}^{\mathcal{N}}}\bigl[\kappa(x,y)\bigr]\in[0,1], (8)

which is large at strings xx that resemble what the model generates and small elsewhere. Averaging the witness over the target recovers the coupling term. For a function ff on 𝒳\mathcal{X}, we write

Pm​f:=1m​∑i=1mf⁡(xi),P​f:=𝔼x∼p​[f⁡(x)]P_{m}f:=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}f(x_{i}),\qquad Pf:=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p}\bigl[f(x)\bigr] (9)

for its average over the training sample and over the target. In this language, a learned model overfits when its witness is larger on the training strings than on typical target strings, (Pm−P)​hθ^𝒩𝒩>0(P_{m}-P)h^{\mathcal{N}}_{\hat{\theta}_{\mathcal{N}}}>0. Adding a constant to a function does not change this difference,

(Pm−P)​(f+c)=(Pm−P)​f,c∈ℝ,(P_{m}-P)(f+c)=(P_{m}-P)f,\qquad c\in\mathbb{R}, (10)

so constant parts of a witness never contribute to overfitting. The witness class

𝒲𝒩:={hθ𝒩:θ∈Θ},𝒲±𝒩:=𝒲𝒩∪(−𝒲𝒩),\mathcal{W}^{\mathcal{N}}:=\bigl\{h_{\theta}^{\mathcal{N}}:\theta\in\Theta\bigr\},\qquad\mathcal{W}_{\pm}^{\mathcal{N}}:=\mathcal{W}^{\mathcal{N}}\cup\bigl(-\mathcal{W}^{\mathcal{N}}\bigr), (11)

contains one witness for each distribution that the noisy device can reach. It depends on the noise and on which distributions are reachable, but not on how many parameters are used to reach them.

Rademacher complexity.

How much a learned witness can overfit depends on how rich the witness class is. We measure richness with the Rademacher complexity Bartlett and Mendelson (2002),

ℜ⁡(ℱ):=𝔼𝒮∼p⊗m​𝔼σ​[supf∈ℱ1m​∑i=1mσi​f​(xi)],\mathfrak{R}(\mathcal{F}):=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}\sim p^{\otimes m}}\,\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\Bigl[\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sigma_{i}f(x_{i})\Bigr], (12)

where σ1,…,σm\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{m} are independent uniform random signs. Each draw of the signs splits the training strings at random into two groups, and the supremum asks how well some function in ℱ\mathcal{F} can be large on one group and small on the other. A rich class can follow any such random split, and hence the accidental features of a particular sample while a poor class cannot. Every witness has RKHS norm at most one, which implies ℜ⁡(𝒲±𝒩)≤1/m\mathfrak{R}(\mathcal{W}^{\mathcal{N}}_{\pm})\leq 1/\sqrt{m} for any noise process. Our results show how noise lowers the constant in front of 1/m1/\sqrt{m}.

2.2 Residual noise contracts the generalization gap

In this subsection, we bound the generalization gap, first for an arbitrary noise process and then for local Pauli noise, where the effect of noise becomes explicit. Throughout, we make one assumption on the kernel, which exposes the structure on which noise acts.

Assumption 1 (Translation-invariant kernel).

The positive-semidefinite kernel κ:𝒳×𝒳→[0,1]\kappa:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\rightarrow[0,1] satisfies

κ⁡(x,y)=ϕ⁡(x⊕y),ϕ⁡(𝟎)=1,\kappa(x,y)=\phi(x\oplus y),\qquad\phi(\mathbf{0})=1, (13)

for some ϕ:𝒳→[0,1]\phi:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow[0,1].

This assumption covers the Hamming-distance kernels commonly used for MMD training of Born machines, including the Gaussian kernels above Liu and Wang (2018); Coyle et al. (2020). To bound the gap, note that the target–target term in equation (5) does not depend on θ\theta and the model–model term is estimated from samples drawn after training, so only the coupling term contributes (i.e., Δ𝒩​(m)=2​𝔼​[(Pm−P)​hθ^𝒩𝒩]\Delta_{\mathcal{N}}(m)=2\,\mathbb{E}[(P_{m}-P)h^{\mathcal{N}}_{\hat{\theta}_{\mathcal{N}}}]), which does not depend on NN (Lemma 1, Methods). Because the learned witness lies in 𝒲𝒩\mathcal{W}^{\mathcal{N}}, its deviation is at most the largest deviation over the class, which symmetrization bounds by the Rademacher complexity. This gives our first result.

Theorem 1 (Noise-agnostic generalization bound).

Let m≥2m\geq 2 and 𝒜𝒩\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{N}} be any possibly randomized learning algorithm with the noise model 𝒩\mathcal{N}, we have

|Δ𝒩​(m)|≤4​ℜ​(𝒲±𝒩).\left|\Delta_{\mathcal{N}}(m)\right|\leq 4\,\mathfrak{R}\left(\mathcal{W}_{\pm}^{\mathcal{N}}\right). (14)

Theorem 1 separates generalization from the details of the training algorithm and of the noise model. It holds for any noise process, including correlated and readout errors, and all dependence on the noise is captured by the reachable witness class. Therefore, noise improves the bound only when it reduces the complexity of that class. In the rest of this subsection, we quantify how much local Pauli noise reduces it.

Scrambled local Pauli noise.

We now make this reduction explicit for local Pauli noise, a standard model of gate errors into which randomized compiling converts general gate noise Wallman and Emerson (2016). Because noise acts on the output distribution, we first describe how a witness depends on that distribution. Bit strings form a group under bitwise addition, and the corresponding Fourier basis consists of the parities χA​(x):=(−1)∑j∈Axj\chi_{A}(x):=(-1)^{\sum_{j\in A}x_{j}} of subsets A⊆[n]A\subseteq[n] of qubits. We write

ϕ^​(A):=2−n​∑t∈𝒳ϕ⁡(t)​χA​(t),q^​(A):=𝔼x∼q​[χA​(x)]\widehat{\phi}(A):=2^{-n}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{X}}\phi(t)\chi_{A}(t),\qquad\widehat{q}(A):=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim q}\bigl[\chi_{A}(x)\bigr] (15)

for the Fourier coefficients of the kernel and of a distribution qq. The coefficient q^​(A)\widehat{q}(A) is the parity moment of qq on the qubits in AA, that is, the expectation value of the Pauli string ZA=⨂j∈AZjZ_{A}=\bigotimes_{j\in A}Z_{j}, and ϕ^​(A)≥0\widehat{\phi}(A)\geq 0 is the weight that the kernel places on it. Under Assumption 1, a noiseless witness is then a kernel-weighted sum of these moments,

hθ0​(x)=∑A⊆[n]ϕ^​(A)​qθ0^​(A)​χA​(x).h_{\theta}^{0}(x)=\sum_{A\subseteq[n]}\widehat{\phi}(A)\,\widehat{q_{\theta}^{0}}(A)\,\chi_{A}(x). (16)

The term with A=∅A=\varnothing equals the same constant ϕ^​(∅)\widehat{\phi}(\varnothing) for every generator, so by equation (10) it cannot cause overfitting. Therefore, overfitting can arise only from the nonconstant moments, and these are exactly what noise erodes.

Consider a circuit of ss two-qubit gates in which every gate is followed by local stochastic Pauli errors of rate ϵ\epsilon on the qubits it acts on. Although each error is local, a sufficiently scrambling circuit spreads it over the entire output distribution. Dalzell et al. Dalzell et al. (2024) showed that, for random circuits under weak local noise, the output distribution is close to a mixture of the ideal and uniform distributions, with effective noise rate γ=1−exp⁡(−2​s​ϵ±𝒪⁡(s​ϵ2))\gamma=1-\exp(-2s\epsilon\pm\mathcal{O}(s\epsilon^{2})) and an approximation error of order (1−γ)​ϵ​s(1-\gamma)\epsilon\sqrt{s}. Such white-noise models are also commonly used to describe the accumulated noise of hardware Vovrosh et al. (2021); Urbanek et al. (2021). We adopt this description for the circuits we train and measure its error in the geometry of the loss.

Assumption 2 (Scrambled local Pauli noise).

Suppose that each circuit contains ss two-qubit gates, each followed by local Pauli errors of rate ϵ\epsilon on both of its qubits. The circuit family scrambles these errors sufficiently that the resulting output distribution is uniformly approximated by an effective white-noise model. Specifically, there exist an effective noise rate γ∈[0,1]\gamma\in[0,1] and a constant cscr>0c_{\mathrm{scr}}>0 such that

qθγ​(x)\displaystyle q_{\theta}^{\gamma}(x) :=(1−γ)​qθ0​(x)+γ​u​(x),u⁡(x)=2−n,\displaystyle:=(1-\gamma)q_{\theta}^{0}(x)+\gamma u(x),\qquad u(x)=2^{-n}, (17)
supθ∈ΘMMDκ⁡(qθ𝒩,qθγ)\displaystyle\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\operatorname{MMD}_{\kappa}\left(q_{\theta}^{\mathcal{N}},q_{\theta}^{\gamma}\right) ≤cscr​(1−γ)​ϵ​s=:εPauli.\displaystyle\leq c_{\mathrm{scr}}(1-\gamma)\epsilon\sqrt{s}=:\varepsilon_{\mathrm{Pauli}}. (18)

Since trained circuits are not random, this is a modelling assumption about the circuit family. Because the uniform distribution has no nonconstant parity moments, white noise scales every nonconstant moment, and hence the part of every witness that can overfit, by 1−γ1-\gamma. The part of the physical noise that is not white changes each witness by at most εPauli\varepsilon_{\mathrm{Pauli}} in RKHS norm (Methods). Combining these two facts with Theorem 1 gives our main generalization result.

Theorem 2 (Generalization under scrambled local Pauli noise).

Suppose that Assumptions 1 and 2 hold and that, for some C≥1C\geq 1,

supθ∈Θ2n​∑x∈𝒳qθ0​(x)2≤C.\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}2^{n}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}q_{\theta}^{0}(x)^{2}\leq C. (19)

Let m,N≥2m,N\geq 2. Then the expected generalization gap satisfies

|Δ𝒩​(m)|≤4​(1−γ)​ΛCm+2​εPaulim,\left|\Delta_{\mathcal{N}}(m)\right|\leq 4(1-\gamma)\frac{\Lambda_{C}}{\sqrt{m}}+\frac{2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{Pauli}}}{\sqrt{m}}, (20)

where ΛC:=min⁡{(C−1)​∑A≠∅ϕ^​(A)2, 1−ϕ^​(∅)}\Lambda_{C}:=\min\bigl\{\sqrt{(C-1)\sum_{A\neq\varnothing}\widehat{\phi}(A)^{2}},\,1-\widehat{\phi}(\varnothing)\bigr\}.

Theorem 2 makes the effect of noise explicit. The constant ΛC\Lambda_{C} is the complexity of the noiseless witness class. In its first branch, C−1C-1 bounds the total squared magnitude of the nonconstant parity moments that the circuits can reach, which vanishes for the uniform distribution and grows as the outputs concentrate, and ∑A≠∅ϕ^​(A)2\sum_{A\neq\varnothing}\widehat{\phi}(A)^{2} measures how strongly the loss weighs those moments. Because CC can be as large as 2n2^{n}, for example when the circuit can output a single bit string, the second branch caps the complexity of every circuit family at a constant below one. Neither branch depends on the number of parameters, unlike supervised quantum learning bounds that grow with the number of trainable gates Caro et al. (2022). White noise contracts this complexity by the retained-signal factor 1−γ1-\gamma. Specifically, uniform samples carry no information about which strings appeared in training, so retained noise dilutes the part of the model that can memorize them, as if a noiseless model were trained on m/(1−γ)2m/(1-\gamma)^{2} samples. Noise that is not white enters only through εPauli\varepsilon_{\mathrm{Pauli}}, which also decays as m−1/2m^{-1/2}. Therefore, noise helps generalization to the extent that it acts as white noise, and this holds not only on average but for a single training run.

Corollary 1 (High-probability generalization bound).

Under the conditions of Theorem 2, for every β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1), with probability at least 1−β1-\beta over 𝒮\mathcal{S}, 𝒜𝒩\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{N}}, and 𝒴\mathcal{Y},

|R𝒩​(θ^𝒩)−R^𝒮,𝒴𝒩​(θ^𝒩)|\displaystyle\left|R_{\mathcal{N}}(\hat{\theta}_{\mathcal{N}})-\widehat{R}_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{Y}}^{\mathcal{N}}(\hat{\theta}_{\mathcal{N}})\right| ≤4​(1−γ)​ΛCm+2​(1−γ)​2​log⁡(4/β)m\displaystyle\leq 4(1-\gamma)\frac{\Lambda_{C}}{\sqrt{m}}+2(1-\gamma)\sqrt{\frac{2\log(4/\beta)}{m}}
+2​εPaulim​(1+2​log⁡(4/β))+log⁡(8/β)2​⌊m/2⌋+8​log⁡(8/β)N.\displaystyle\quad+\frac{2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{Pauli}}}{\sqrt{m}}\left(1+\sqrt{2\log(4/\beta)}\right)+\sqrt{\frac{\log(8/\beta)}{2\lfloor m/2\rfloor}}+\sqrt{\frac{8\log(8/\beta)}{N}}. (21)

Corollary 1 adds two observations to Theorem 2. First, the first three terms all carry the factor 1−γ1-\gamma, the third through εPauli\varepsilon_{\mathrm{Pauli}}, so noise reduces not only the expected gap but also its fluctuation across draws of the training sample, and a single-run guarantee costs only a logarithmic factor in 1/β1/\beta. Second, the last two terms do not depend on γ\gamma. They come from estimating the target–target term with mm samples and the model-dependent terms with NN evaluation shots, and they form a floor of order log⁡(1/β)/m+log⁡(1/β)/N\sqrt{\log(1/\beta)/m}+\sqrt{\log(1/\beta)/N} that no amount of noise can lower. The shot term can be made negligible by measuring more, so the floor that remains is set by the training data. Because the contracted terms and this floor both decay as m−1/2m^{-1/2}, their ratio does not depend on mm. In terms of the bound, noise therefore yields a substantial reduction only while (1−γ)​ΛC(1-\gamma)\Lambda_{C} exceeds log⁡(1/β)\sqrt{\log(1/\beta)} up to constants, which favours expressive circuit families with concentrated outputs, precisely the models most prone to overfitting. Beyond that point, additional noise barely shrinks the gap but still pulls the model towards the uniform distribution, a cost we quantify in the next subsection.

2.3 Realizing a target noise level by capped error reduction

The previous subsection shows that retained noise contracts the bound on the generalization gap. Noise, however, also changes the model itself. Under the white-noise model, μqθγ=(1−γ)​μqθ0+γ​μu\mu_{q^{\gamma}_{\theta}}=(1-\gamma)\mu_{q^{0}_{\theta}}+\gamma\mu_{u}, so the population loss becomes

MMDκ2​(qθγ,p)=‖(μqθ0−μp)−γ⁡(μqθ0−μu)‖ℋ2.\mathrm{MMD}^{2}_{\kappa}\bigl(q^{\gamma}_{\theta},p\bigr)=\left\lVert\bigl(\mu_{q^{0}_{\theta}}-\mu_{p}\bigr)-\gamma\bigl(\mu_{q^{0}_{\theta}}-\mu_{u}\bigr)\right\rVert_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}. (22)

Noise thus pulls the kernel mean embedding of the model towards that of the uniform distribution, and even a perfect fit, qθ0=pq^{0}_{\theta}=p, incurs the loss γ2​MMDκ2​(p,u)\gamma^{2}\mathrm{MMD}^{2}_{\kappa}(p,u). The effective noise level therefore acts as a regularization parameter that trades a smaller gap against the loss of the nonuniform structure the target requires, and its best value can be intermediate.

Therefore, using noise as a regularizer raises two practical questions. The first is how to realize a chosen noise level. The hardware supplies a fixed amount of noise, so a lower level can only be reached by removing part of it with error mitigation. The second is which level to choose, because the best value is not known before training. In this work, we propose GENIE, a noise-based regularization framework that answers these two questions with two components (see Fig. 1 for an overview). In this subsection, we present the first component, capped probabilistic error reduction (capped PER), which realizes a target noise level by removing just enough hardware noise while keeping the remaining noise close to white noise.

Residual noise and its cost.

We start from the characterized hardware profile ϵ\boldsymbol{\epsilon} of equation (3). To lower the noise, we choose a residual profile 𝐫=(r1,…,rL)\mathbf{r}=(r_{1},\ldots,r_{L}) with 0≤rk≤ϵk0\leq r_{k}\leq\epsilon_{k}, which keeps each πk\pi_{k} but reduces its rate to rkr_{k}. We implement it with probabilistic error reduction (PER) Mari et al. (2021), the partial variant of probabilistic error cancellation Temme et al. (2017); van den Berg et al. (2023). PER inserts randomly sampled Pauli corrections and attaches to each measurement outcome a signed weight of magnitude Γ⁡(𝐫)\Gamma(\mathbf{r}). Weighted averages are then unbiased for expectation values under the residual noise, with a standard error that grows as Γ⁡(𝐫)/N\Gamma(\mathbf{r})/\sqrt{N}. In the weak-noise regime, this cost takes a simple form (Lemma 3, Methods),

Γ⁡(𝐫)≃exp⁡(2​‖ϵ−𝐫‖1).\Gamma(\mathbf{r})\simeq\exp\bigl(2\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\mathbf{r}\right\rVert_{1}\bigr). (23)

The cost depends only on the total amount of noise removed, and it grows exponentially with it. The MMD is more expensive still, because its model–model term multiplies two weights, so a fixed precision can require about Γ​(𝐫)4\Gamma(\mathbf{r})^{4} times more circuit executions than without mitigation. Every unit of noise that we keep therefore saves an exponential number of executions.

Effective noise of a residual profile.

To connect a residual profile to Theorem 2, we assume Assumption 2 in a profile-dependent form. Writing qθ𝐫q_{\theta}^{\mathbf{r}} for the output distribution under 𝐫\mathbf{r}, its effective noise level and its distance from white noise are

γ⁡(𝐫)\displaystyle\gamma(\mathbf{r}) :=1−exp⁡(−‖𝐫‖1),\displaystyle:=1-\exp\bigl(-\left\lVert\mathbf{r}\right\rVert_{1}\bigr), (24)
supθ∈ΘMMDκ​(qθ𝐫,qθγ⁡(𝐫))\displaystyle\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathrm{MMD}_{\kappa}\bigl(q_{\theta}^{\mathbf{r}},q_{\theta}^{\gamma(\mathbf{r})}\bigr) ≤cscr​exp⁡(−‖𝐫‖1)​‖𝐫‖2,\displaystyle\leq c_{\mathrm{scr}}\exp\bigl(-\left\lVert\mathbf{r}\right\rVert_{1}\bigr)\left\lVert\mathbf{r}\right\rVert_{2}, (25)

which recovers the scaling of Assumption 2 for homogeneous rates up to a constant factor. Like the cost, the effective level depends only on the total retained noise ‖𝐫‖1\left\lVert\mathbf{r}\right\rVert_{1}. The distance from white noise, in contrast, also depends on how the retained noise is spread across the circuit, through ‖𝐫‖2\left\lVert\mathbf{r}\right\rVert_{2}. Where the noise is kept therefore matters only for how white it is.

Capped allocation problem.

We can now state the design problem that capped PER solves. A target γ⋆\gamma_{\star} specifies the largest effective noise level we are willing to keep. Many residual profiles stay within this level, and they differ in two respects that matter, namely how much mitigation they require and how close their remaining noise is to white noise. We therefore seek the residual profile that meets the target at the lowest cost while keeping its distance from white noise below a tolerance εtol\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tol}},

min𝐫∈ℝLexp⁡(2​‖ϵ−𝐫‖1)subject to1−exp⁡(−‖𝐫‖1)≤γ⋆,cscr​exp⁡(−‖𝐫‖1)​‖𝐫‖2≤εtol,0≤rk≤ϵk,k=1,…,L.\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \min_{\mathbf{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{L}}\quad&\exp\left(2\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\mathbf{r}\right\rVert_{1}\right)\\ \text{subject to}\quad&1-\exp\left(-\left\lVert\mathbf{r}\right\rVert_{1}\right)\leq\gamma_{\star},\\ &c_{\mathrm{scr}}\exp\left(-\left\lVert\mathbf{r}\right\rVert_{1}\right)\left\lVert\mathbf{r}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tol}},\\ &0\leq r_{k}\leq\epsilon_{k},\qquad k=1,\ldots,L.\end{aligned} (26)

Because the cost and the level depend only on R:=‖𝐫‖1R:=\left\lVert\mathbf{r}\right\rVert_{1}, the problem separates into deciding how much noise to keep and deciding where to keep it. For a fixed total RR, the profile closest to white noise is the capped allocation (Lemma 4, Methods)

rkcap​(R)=min⁡{ϵk,ν⁡(R)},∑k=1Lmin⁡{ϵk,ν⁡(R)}=R.r^{\mathrm{cap}}_{k}(R)=\min\{\epsilon_{k},\nu(R)\},\qquad\sum_{k=1}^{L}\min\{\epsilon_{k},\nu(R)\}=R. (27)

It lowers the noisiest locations to a common level ν⁡(R)\nu(R) and leaves the quieter ones untouched, so mitigation is spent only where the noise is concentrated. Capped PER then keeps the largest total noise that meets both requirements,

Rmax\displaystyle R_{\max} :=min⁡{‖ϵ‖1,log⁡11−γ⋆},\displaystyle:=\min\Bigl\{\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\right\rVert_{1},\ \log\frac{1}{1-\gamma_{\star}}\Bigr\}, (28)
R⋆\displaystyle R^{\star} :=max⁡{R∈[0,Rmax]|cscr​e−R​‖𝐫cap​(R)‖2≤εtol},\displaystyle:=\max\Bigl\{R\in[0,R_{\max}]\ \Big|\ c_{\mathrm{scr}}\,e^{-R}\left\lVert\mathbf{r}^{\mathrm{cap}}(R)\right\rVert_{2}\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tol}}\Bigr\}, (29)

and implements the profile 𝐫⋆=𝐫cap​(R⋆)\mathbf{r}^{\star}=\mathbf{r}^{\mathrm{cap}}(R^{\star}) with PER (Algorithm 1, Methods). The result has effective level γout=1−e−R⋆≤γ⋆\gamma_{\mathrm{out}}=1-e^{-R^{\star}}\leq\gamma_{\star} and cost Γ⋆=exp⁡[2​(‖ϵ‖1−R⋆)]\Gamma^{\star}=\exp[2(\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\right\rVert_{1}-R^{\star})]. When the profile that reaches γ⋆\gamma_{\star} is too far from white noise, capped PER mitigates beyond the target, giving the validity of the white-noise description priority over cost.

Below the hardware noise level, the PER weights make the Born machine a quasi-probability model that is accessed through weighted expectation values rather than samples van den Berg et al. (2023); Cai et al. (2023). The MMD estimates and gradients used in training are such expectations, which we obtain by executing many randomly sampled PER circuits and combining their outcomes with the known weights. At the hardware level no mitigation is applied, and the model can be sampled directly. Capped PER thus turns any target noise level into an implementable residual profile with a known cost, which leaves open the question of which level to target.

2.4 Budget-aware noise-control regularization framework

Capped PER realizes any target noise level, which leaves the second question of which level to target. The best level balances the contraction of the gap in Theorem 2 against the bias in equation (22) and the mitigation cost in equation (23). This balance depends on the target distribution and on the model being trained, neither of which is known in advance, so the level cannot be fixed before training. The second component of GENIE therefore selects it during training, by comparing candidate levels on held-out data within a fixed budget of circuit executions. In this subsection, we formulate this selection problem, describe the controller that solves it, and bound the regret of its decisions.

Noise allocation problem.

For a residual profile 𝐫\mathbf{r}, let R𝐫​(θ):=MMDκ2​(p,qθ𝐫)R_{\mathbf{r}}(\theta):=\mathrm{MMD}_{\kappa}^{2}(p,q_{\theta}^{\mathbf{r}}) denote the population loss under that profile. As discussed in the first subsection, this loss equals the training loss plus the generalization gap, so minimizing it accounts for both fit and generalization. Training performs TT parameter updates within a total budget of BB circuit executions. A policy π\pi chooses, at each step tt, a residual profile 𝐫tπ\mathbf{r}^{\pi}_{t} from the set ℛtol\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{tol}} of profiles produced by capped PER and a number NtπN^{\pi}_{t} of shots per training circuit. At the comparison steps t∈ℐt\in\mathcal{I}, it also chooses a number Mt​jπM^{\pi}_{tj} of probe shots for each candidate profile jj. Its objective is

minimize𝜋\displaystyle\underset{\pi}{\operatorname{minimize}}\quad 𝔼⁡[R𝐫^π​(θ^π)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[R_{\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{\pi}}(\hat{\theta}^{\pi})\right]
subject to ∑t=0T−1Pcirc​Ntπ+∑t∈ℐ∑j∈𝒥tMt​jπ≤B,\displaystyle\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}P_{\mathrm{circ}}N_{t}^{\pi}+\sum_{t\in\mathcal{I}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{t}}M_{tj}^{\pi}\leq B,
𝐫tπ∈ℛtol,t=0,…,T−1.\displaystyle\mathbf{r}_{t}^{\pi}\in\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{tol}},\qquad t=0,\ldots,T-1. (30)

where Pcirc=1+2​dim(θ)P_{\mathrm{circ}}=1+2\dim(\theta) is the number of circuits per parameter-shift update. The constraint counts circuit executions, whereas the PER normalization determines how precise each execution is. A policy must therefore divide a single budget among the noise level, the precision of the training updates, and the comparisons between candidates.

Noise selection from held-out data.

Because the population loss is unknown and depends on the whole training trajectory, we address equation (30) with a practical policy that periodically compares candidate noise levels on held-out data (Algorithm 2 in Methods). Applying capped PER to a grid of target levels gives JJ candidate profiles 𝐫(j)\mathbf{r}^{(j)} with effective levels γj=1−exp⁡(−‖𝐫(j)‖1)\gamma_{j}=1-\exp(-\left\lVert\mathbf{r}^{(j)}\right\rVert_{1}) and normalizations Γj=Γ⁡(𝐫(j))\Gamma_{j}=\Gamma(\mathbf{r}^{(j)}). A fraction α\alpha of the budget is reserved for comparisons and the rest for training, which is spread evenly so that each remaining training circuit receives Nfuture,tN_{\mathrm{future},t} shots. Every KK steps, the controller holds the parameters θt\theta_{t} fixed, probes every candidate with MtM_{t} fresh PER executions, and estimates its MMD to a held-out validation sample of size vv with a weighted U-statistic L~val,tU​(j)\widetilde{L}^{U}_{\mathrm{val},t}(j) (Methods). It then selects

jt∈arg⁡minj∈𝒥​{L~val,tU​(j)⏟validation fit+bt​j⏟measurement radius+λ​Γj2Nfuture,t⏟budget lookahead}j_{t}\in\arg\min_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\Bigl\{\underbrace{\widetilde{L}^{U}_{\mathrm{val},t}(j)}_{\text{validation fit}}+\underbrace{b_{tj}}_{\text{measurement radius}}+\underbrace{\lambda\,\frac{\Gamma_{j}^{2}}{N_{\mathrm{future},t}}}_{\text{budget lookahead}}\Bigr\} (31)

and keeps the profile 𝐫(jt)\mathbf{r}^{(j_{t})} until the next comparison. The validation fit is an empirical proxy for the population loss at the current parameters. The measurement radius bt​j:=z​SE^​(L~val,tU​(j))b_{tj}:=z\,\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\widetilde{L}^{U}_{\mathrm{val},t}(j)), with z≥0z\geq 0, keeps the controller from choosing a strongly mitigated candidate on the strength of a low but imprecise estimate. The budget lookahead penalizes candidates whose mitigation cost would leave too few shots for later training, and it relaxes as the remaining allowance grows. Training starts from the candidate with the largest γj\gamma_{j}, which is the cheapest, so noise is removed only when the validation evidence justifies its cost. Because the validation sample is reused across comparisons, final performance is assessed on an independent test set.

Cumulative selection regret.

To assess these decisions, we compare the controller with the best candidate at every training step, with all candidates evaluated at the same current parameters,

Ψt​(j):=R𝐫(j)​(θt)+λ​Γj2Nfuture,t,RegT:=∑t=0T−1[Ψt​(jt)−minj∈𝒥⁡Ψt​(j)].\Psi_{t}(j):=R_{\mathbf{r}^{(j)}}(\theta_{t})+\lambda\,\frac{\Gamma_{j}^{2}}{N_{\mathrm{future},t}},\qquad\mathrm{Reg}_{T}:=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\Bigl[\Psi_{t}(j_{t})-\min_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\Psi_{t}(j)\Bigr]. (32)

The regret reflects both the accuracy of each comparison and the cost of keeping a profile while the parameters change. Its analysis rests on three facts. First, capped PER keeps every candidate within εtol\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tol}} of its white-noise model by equation (25), so candidates differ mainly through their effective levels. Second, if each of the dθd_{\theta} parameters enters once through a Pauli rotation, the loss changes with the parameters at a rate of at most LR:=2​2​dθL_{R}:=2\sqrt{2d_{\theta}} (Lemma 5, Methods). Third, the parameters themselves change slowly.

Assumption 3 (Controlled updates).

For a constant h>0h>0 independent of TT,

∥θt+1−θt∥2≤ht+1,t=0,…,T−1.\|\theta_{t+1}-\theta_{t}\|_{2}\leq\frac{h}{t+1},\qquad t=0,\ldots,T-1. (33)

Assumption 3 holds for stochastic gradient descent with step size η0/(t+1)\eta_{0}/(t+1) and gradient estimates bounded by GG, with h=η0​Gh=\eta_{0}G Bottou et al. (2018). It also holds approximately for Adam with the same decay, whose per-coordinate steps are bounded by a constant multiple of the learning rate Kingma and Ba (2015). The bound is stated in terms of a few quantities of the run. Comparisons occur at ℐ={0,K,2​K,…}∩{0,…,T−1}\mathcal{I}=\{0,K,2K,\ldots\}\cap\{0,\ldots,T-1\}, which gives H=⌈T/K⌉H=\lceil T/K\rceil rounds, and the comparison at step ss governs the next ws:=min⁡{K,T−s}w_{s}:=\min\{K,T-s\} steps. We write Γ¯:=maxj⁡Γj\overline{\Gamma}:=\max_{j}\Gamma_{j} for the largest normalization, δγ:=maxj⁡γj−minj⁡γj\delta_{\gamma}:=\max_{j}\gamma_{j}-\min_{j}\gamma_{j} for the range of candidate levels, and Ds:=MMDκ​(qθs0,u)D_{s}:=\mathrm{MMD}_{\kappa}(q^{0}_{\theta_{s}},u) for how far the noiseless generator is from uniform at step ss. Finally, av(β):=v−1/2+2​log⁡(2/β)/va_{v}(\beta):=v^{-1/2}+\sqrt{2\log(2/\beta)/v} bounds the error of the validation kernel mean embedding with probability at least 1−β/21-\beta/2.

Theorem 3 (Cumulative selection regret).

Under Assumptions 2 and 3, let T≥2T\geq 2 and 1≤K≤T1\leq K\leq T. Algorithm 2 satisfies, with probability at least 1−β1-\beta,

RegT≤\displaystyle\operatorname{Reg}_{T}\leq{} (15+6​z)​Γ¯2​T​J​H​log⁡(8​J​H/β)α​B+2​av​(β)​(δγ​∑s∈ℐws​Ds+2​T​εtol)\displaystyle(15+6z)\,\overline{\Gamma}^{2}T\sqrt{\frac{JH\log(8JH/\beta)}{\alpha B}}+2a_{v}(\beta)\left(\delta_{\gamma}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{I}}w_{s}D_{s}+2T\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tol}}\right)
+2​(K−1)​[LR​h​(1+log⁡T)+λ​Γ¯2Nfuture,0].\displaystyle+2(K-1)\left[L_{R}h(1+\log T)+\frac{\lambda\overline{\Gamma}^{2}}{N_{\mathrm{future},0}}\right]. (34)

Theorem 3 separates three sources of regret. The first term comes from comparing candidates with finite probe shots and from the measurement radius. It shrinks with the probe budget α​B\alpha B and grows with the number of candidates and comparison rounds, and its factor Γ¯2\overline{\Gamma}^{2} shows that strongly mitigated candidates are expensive to compare, not only to train. The second term comes from the finite validation sample. It is scaled by how different the candidates actually are, so comparisons are robust when the generator is close to uniform or the candidate levels are similar. Because reusing the validation sample supplies no new target data, this term grows linearly in TT however many probe shots are spent. The last term is the price of holding a profile for KK steps while the loss and the training allowance change, and it vanishes for K=1K=1. A larger probe fraction α\alpha sharpens comparisons but leaves fewer executions for training, which is the budget tradeoff of equation (30). Balancing the first and last terms through the comparison interval yields a sublinear rate.

Corollary 2 (Rate under a linear execution budget).

Suppose B=Θ⁡(T)B=\Theta(T) and choose K=⌈T2/3⌉K=\lceil T^{2/3}\rceil. For fixed circuit size, candidate grid, hh, α\alpha, λ\lambda, zz, and εtol\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tol}}, with probability at least 1−β1-\beta,

RegT=𝒪~​(T2/3+Tv),\operatorname{Reg}_{T}=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\!\left(T^{2/3}+\frac{T}{\sqrt{v}}\right), (35)

where 𝒪~\widetilde{\mathcal{O}} suppresses logarithmic factors in TT and 1/β1/\beta.

The interval K=⌈T2/3⌉K=\lceil T^{2/3}\rceil balances the precision gained from less frequent comparisons against the cost of acting on stale ones. At fixed confidence, the average regret RegT/T\mathrm{Reg}_{T}/T then decays as 𝒪(T−1/3logT+v−1/2)\mathcal{O}(T^{-1/3}\log T+v^{-1/2}). The errors from finite probes and delayed comparisons therefore vanish as training proceeds, whereas a fixed validation set leaves a floor of order v−1/2v^{-1/2}. Ultimately, it is the amount of held-out data, not the number of shots, that limits how well the noise level can be selected.

2.5 Numerical Demonstrations

2.5.1 Experiments on Synthetic Datasets

Loss across training-set sizes and execution budgets

.

Figure 2 shows the final population loss LPL_{P} of each method as a function of the training-set size mm, with one panel per execution budget and the three error rates averaged. The vertical axis is shared across the four panels of each target, so reading a row from left to right shows how each method converts additional executions into a better model. Overall, GENIE gives the lowest loss of the four methods. On blob and wfc, it is the best method, or tied with the best within the seed range, in every panel. On Ising, it is among the best methods in every panel.

The clearest pattern is that the ranking of the fixed noise levels reverses as the budget grows. At the smallest budget, full mitigation is the worst on all three targets, because its PER estimates are Γ2\Gamma^{2} times noisier and few executions cannot average this out. With more executions, the mitigated methods keep improving, while training without mitigation stalls on blob and wfc, because its noise-induced bias (equation (22)) does not shrink with more shots. Beyond the smallest budget, keeping all hardware noise is therefore the worst choice on these targets. No fixed level works well at every budget.

GENIE avoids this problem because it chooses the noise level from data. When executions are scarce, it keeps most of the hardware noise, as training without mitigation does. When executions are plentiful, it removes most of the noise, as full mitigation does. At the intermediate budgets, it does better than all three fixed levels, possibly because it can use levels between them or change the level during training. On Ising, the four methods are close and their seed ranges overlap, so the differences there are small.

Finally, the training-set size matters less than the budget. For most methods, the loss drops between m=64m=64 and m=256m=256 and changes little afterwards. On blob and wfc, the ranking of the methods also stays the same across mm. In this range of mm, the best noise level is therefore decided mainly by the budget and the error rate rather than by the amount of training data. Ising depends more strongly on mm at large budgets.

Regret across all conditions

To compare the methods over the whole grid, we compute in each of the 144144 conditions (i.e., combinations of target, error rate, training-set size and budget). The regret is the percentage by which a method’s loss exceeds that of the best of the four methods in that condition (Methods). It also differs from the cumulative selection regret RegT\mathrm{Reg}_{T} of Theorem 3, which sums, over the steps of a single training run, how much worse the level chosen by the controller is than the best candidate level. Figure 3 summarizes the regrets. GENIE has a median regret of 0.3%0.3\% and a mean regret of 3.8%3.8\%, far below every fixed level. Full and half mitigation have median regrets of about 8.5%8.5\% and mean regrets of 11.7%11.7\% and 14.8%14.8\%, and training without mitigation is the worst, with a median of 22.7%22.7\% and a mean of 33.0%33.0\%. For every method the mean exceeds the median, because regret cannot be negative and a few large regrets pull the mean up.

Two summary numbers can hide how often a method fails, so Fig. 4 shows the full picture. Panel a plots, for each regret threshold xx, the percentage of conditions in which a method is within x%x\% of the best method. The curve of GENIE lies above those of all fixed levels at every threshold, so its advantage does not rest on a few favourable conditions. GENIE is within 1%1\% of the best method in 64%64\% of conditions and within 5%5\% in 78%78\%, whereas no fixed level exceeds 29%29\% and 42%42\% at these thresholds.

Panel b counts how often each method is the best and how often it is the worst in its condition. GENIE is the best method in 43%43\% of conditions and the worst in only 2%2\%. The fixed levels are risky in different ways. Full mitigation has a moderate mean regret but is the worst method in 38%38\% of conditions, and training without mitigation is the worst in 57%57\%. Half mitigation is rarely the worst (3%3\%) but also rarely the best (15%15\%).

Therefore, no fixed noise level is safe to use in practice. Each one performs badly in a sizeable fraction of conditions, and which conditions those are depends on the error rate and the budget at hand. In contrast, GENIE is not always the best method, but it is almost never far from the best.

2.5.2 Experiments on a Real Census Dataset

The synthetic experiments evaluate distributional fit through population MMD loss. To assess whether these improvements translate into more accurate population statistics and better predictions, we repeat the comparison on the Adult census dataset Becker and Kohavi (1996). Each 1010-bit string encodes a person’s record through seven attributes, including whether their income exceeds $50K (Methods). We evaluate the learned distributions against held-out real records using three practical criteria: the shares of people satisfying individual attributes, income rates within demographic subgroups, and the accuracy of income predictions for unseen individuals. These evaluations test whether lower MMD loss corresponds to better preservation of interpretable features of the data distribution.

Population shares.

We first evaluate whether generated samples reproduce the marginal probabilities of seven demographic and socioeconomic events in the Adult dataset. For each event, such as earning above $50K, we compare the fraction of generated records satisfying that event with the corresponding fraction in the held-out real data. Figure 5 shows these fractions. In details, the gap between a method’s bar and the dotted reference line is its absolute error for that event.

GENIE achieves the smallest error, or ties for the smallest, on six of the seven events. The exception is the share of married people, where GENIE is two points below the real share and the other methods are within one point. For example, without mitigation, 43%43\% of generated records have income above $50K, compared with 24%24\% in the real data. GENIE reduces this share to 32%32\%. Similarly, it reduces the generated share of managers or professionals from 43%43\% to 31%31\%, closer to the real share of 25%25\%. Averaged over the seven events, the absolute discrepancy is approximately 44 percentage points for GENIE, compared with 88–1010 percentage points for the fixed mitigation levels. All methods closely match the shares of married people and people with a bachelor’s degree or higher, so these two events provide little separation between methods.

Income rates within groups.

Matching marginal population shares does not ensure that a model preserves relationships between attributes. Therefore, we evaluate conditional income rates. Specifically, the rate is the fraction of records earning above $50K within a specified subgroup, such as married men or people aged 2828 or younger without a high-school diploma. We consider 125125 subgroups, each defined by a combination of values of two non-income attributes and containing at least 2%2\% of the real test records. For each subgroup gg, we compare the generated income rate q^g\widehat{q}_{g} with the real test rate p^g\widehat{p}_{g}. We summarize these discrepancies using the group-size-weighted mean absolute error,

Erate=∑g∈𝒢ng​|q^g−p^g|∑g∈𝒢ng,E_{\mathrm{rate}}=\frac{\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}n_{g}\left|\widehat{q}_{g}-\widehat{p}_{g}\right|}{\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}n_{g}},

where ngn_{g} is the number of real test records in subgroup gg. The subgroups may overlap. The weighting gives greater importance to errors on larger groups.

Figure 6 plots the generated rate against the real rate for each subgroup, with the diagonal indicating exact agreement. The real rates range from approximately 0%0\% to 70%70\%. Without mitigation, many generated rates cluster near 50%50\%, including for groups whose real rates are much lower. The fixed mitigation levels also overestimate income rates for many low-income groups, while full mitigation exhibits substantial variation across seeds. GENIE produces lower rates for many of these groups and achieves the lowest weighted mean absolute error with 1616 percentage points, compared with 2121 without mitigation, 1919 with 50%50\% mitigation, and 2222 with full mitigation.

Nevertheless, GENIE does not fully recover the conditional income structure. Many low-income groups remain overestimated, and some high-income groups are underestimated. For context, the same metric is approximately 2828 percentage points for a uniform distribution over encoded records and less than 11 percentage point for the empirical training distribution. Thus, GENIE improves conditional fidelity under the available measurement budget, but a gap remains relative to the relationships present in the training data.

Income prediction for real people.

We next evaluate whether the learned distribution supports income prediction on unseen real records. For each test record, we condition on its nine non-income bits and use the model’s conditional probability of the income bit to predict whether income exceeds $50K, following the decision rule in Methods. This predictor is read directly from the learned distribution.

Figure 7 partitions the real test records into three outcomes including correct predictions, false positives (income at most $50K predicted as above $50K), and false negatives (income above $50K predicted as at most $50K). Each bar reports these outcomes per 100100 test records. GENIE correctly classifies approximately 6868 records, compared with 6161 without mitigation, 5757 with 50%50\% mitigation, and 5858 with full mitigation. This improvement comes primarily from fewer false positives, which are, 1919 per 100100 records for GENIE, versus 2626–3030 for the fixed mitigation levels. All four methods produce approximately 1313 false negatives per 100100 records at the displayed precision.

3 Discussion

In this work, we have shown that the residual noise of a quantum circuit Born machine acts as a regularizer whose strength can be quantified, realized on hardware and chosen during training. The analysis rests on an identity that reduces the generalization gap of an MMD-trained Born machine to the overfitting of its witness function, so that for any noise process the gap is controlled by the complexity of the witness class (Theorem 1). For scrambled local Pauli noise, this complexity contracts by the retained-signal factor 1−γ1-\gamma (Theorem 2). The best noise level can be intermediate and unknown before training. GENIE turns this trade-off into a procedure. Capped probabilistic error reduction realizes any target level at the lowest mitigation cost while keeping the remaining noise close to white noise, and a budget-aware controller selects the level from held-out data with an average regret per step that decays as T−1/3T^{-1/3} up to a floor of order v−1/2v^{-1/2} set by the held-out sample size (Theorem 3 and Corollary 2).

These results add a second consideration to how error mitigation is used. Mitigation is usually judged by how much bias it removes at a given sampling cost Cai et al. (2023). When a generative model is trained under a fixed budget of circuit executions, however, mitigation buys noisier shots rather than fewer of them, and the noise it removes no longer regularizes the model. How much noise to remove then becomes a model-selection problem that depends on the target, the training data and the budget. Our simulations show what is at stake. Across 144144 synthetic conditions, the fixed noise levels had median regrets of 8.4%8.4\% to 22.7%22.7\% relative to the best of the four methods, and each was the worst method in some conditions, whereas GENIE had a median regret of 0.3%0.3\%. On the Adult census data at strong noise, it gave the most accurate population shares, income rates and income predictions of the four methods. This view parallels the use of injected noise as a regularizer in classical learning Bishop (1995); Srivastava et al. (2014) and the finite optimal noise levels found for supervised quantum models Heyraud et al. (2022); Bu et al. (2023); Zhang et al. (2026). For a Born machine, however, the noisy output distribution is itself the model, so the regularizer carries a bias that we quantify and that the controller weighs against the reduction of the gap.

Our study has three remaining limitations. First, the effective depolarizing approximation underlying Theorem 2 and the controller requires sufficient circuit scrambling to keep the approximation error small. Thus, its precision on estimating the amount of residual noise depends on the circuit architecture and depth. Second, the controller compares candidate noise levels at its current parameters rather than planning a schedule for the whole run, and the reliability of its choices depends on the held-out sample size. In the census experiment, held-out samples of 1313 to 102102 people were already sufficient for GENIE to select useful noise levels. Finally, all experiments use simulated circuits of 1010 and 1212 qubits.

These limitations suggest several natural extensions. Testing GENIE on larger circuits and hardware would help assess the effective depolarizing approximation and the benefits of noise control under realistic conditions. Randomized compiling and sparse noise learning provide tools for tailoring and characterizing the Pauli channels used by capped probabilistic error reduction Wallman and Emerson (2016); van den Berg et al. (2023), allowing the mismatch εPauli\varepsilon_{\mathrm{Pauli}} to be assessed along training trajectories. On the theory side, Theorem 1 covers arbitrary noise processes, while the explicit contraction in Theorem 2 relies on scrambled Pauli noise. Deriving contraction bounds for other channels would clarify which correlations they suppress and when retaining noise is beneficial. More broadly, our results suggest that residual noise, when appropriately characterized and controlled, can serve as a resource for generalization on near-term hardware.

4 Methods

This section collects the technical ingredients behind the Results. We first give the lemmas and proof sketches behind the generalization bounds, then the construction of capped probabilistic error reduction, then the implementation and analysis of the budget-aware controller, and finally the setup of our numerical experiments. Complete proofs are given in Supplementary Note [1].

4.1 Generalization bounds

Reduction to the learned witness.

Both generalization theorems start from an exact identity, which shows that only the coupling term of the MMD can make the empirical risk optimistic.

Lemma 1 (Reduction to the learned witness).

Let m,N≥2m,N\geq 2, and let 𝒜𝒩\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{N}} be any possibly randomized learning algorithm. If the evaluation samples 𝒴\mathcal{Y} are conditionally independent of 𝒮\mathcal{S} and the training randomness given θ^𝒩\hat{\theta}_{\mathcal{N}}, then

Δ𝒩​(m)=2​𝔼𝒮,𝒜𝒩​[(Pm−P)​hθ^𝒩𝒩].\Delta_{\mathcal{N}}(m)=2\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{N}}}\left[(P_{m}-P)h_{\hat{\theta}_{\mathcal{N}}}^{\mathcal{N}}\right]. (36)

Theorem 2 reduces the noisy complexity to that of the centered noiseless witnesses h¯θ:=hθ0−ϕ^​(∅)\bar{h}_{\theta}:=h^{0}_{\theta}-\widehat{\phi}(\varnothing) and their class 𝒲¯±0:={±h¯θ:θ∈Θ}\bar{\mathcal{W}}^{0}_{\pm}:=\{\pm\bar{h}_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\}, which the parity basis makes explicit.

4.2 Capped probabilistic error reduction

This subsection gives the quasi-probability construction behind the cost in equation (23) and the procedure that computes the capped profile.

Quasi-probability implementation.

At location kk, the residual channel with rate rk≤ϵkr_{k}\leq\epsilon_{k} keeps the Pauli distribution of the characterized channel (3),

ℰk,rk​(ρ)=(1−rk)​ρ+rk​∑P∈{X,Y,Z}πk​(P)​P​ρ​P.\mathcal{E}_{k,r_{k}}(\rho)=(1-r_{k})\rho+r_{k}\sum_{P\in\{X,Y,Z\}}\pi_{k}(P)\,P\rho P. (41)

PER implements the correction ℳk,rk:=ℰk,rk∘ℰk−1\mathcal{M}_{k,r_{k}}:=\mathcal{E}_{k,r_{k}}\circ\mathcal{E}_{k}^{-1}. This map is generally not a physical channel, but it can be written as a signed combination of Pauli conjugations, ℳk,rk=∑Pηk,rk​(P)​𝒫\mathcal{M}_{k,r_{k}}=\sum_{P}\eta_{k,r_{k}}(P)\,\mathcal{P} with 𝒫⁡(ρ)=P​ρ​P\mathcal{P}(\rho)=P\rho P. PER samples 𝒫\mathcal{P} with probability proportional to |ηk,rk​(P)||\eta_{k,r_{k}}(P)| and assigns the corresponding outcome the sign of ηk,rk​(P)\eta_{k,r_{k}}(P). Because the corrections are sampled independently across locations, the circuit-level normalization is

Γ⁡(𝐫):=∏k=1LΓk​(rk),Γk​(rk):=∑P|ηk,rk​(P)|,\Gamma(\mathbf{r}):=\prod_{k=1}^{L}\Gamma_{k}(r_{k}),\qquad\Gamma_{k}(r_{k}):=\sum_{P}\bigl|\eta_{k,r_{k}}(P)\bigr|, (42)

and every outcome carries a weight of magnitude Γ⁡(𝐫)\Gamma(\mathbf{r}). The following lemma gives the cost used in the Results.

Lemma 3 (Cost of a mitigation profile).

Suppose that ϵk<1/2\epsilon_{k}<1/2 and 0≤rk≤ϵk0\leq r_{k}\leq\epsilon_{k} for every kk. The circuit-level quasiprobability normalization required to reduce ϵ\boldsymbol{\epsilon} to 𝐫\mathbf{r} satisfies

log⁡Γ⁡(𝐫)=2​‖ϵ−𝐫‖1+𝒪⁡(∑k=1Lϵk​(ϵk−rk)).\log\Gamma(\mathbf{r})=2\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\mathbf{r}\right\rVert_{1}+\mathcal{O}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{L}\epsilon_{k}(\epsilon_{k}-r_{k})\right). (43)

Consequently, in the weak-noise regime,

Γ⁡(𝐫)≃exp⁡(2​‖ϵ−𝐫‖1).\Gamma(\mathbf{r})\simeq\exp\left(2\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\mathbf{r}\right\rVert_{1}\right). (44)

Proof sketch. Each ℳk,rk\mathcal{M}_{k,r_{k}} is diagonal in the Pauli transfer basis. To first order in the rates, ℳk,rk≈id−(ϵk−rk)​∑Pπk​(P)​(𝒫−id)\mathcal{M}_{k,r_{k}}\approx\mathrm{id}-(\epsilon_{k}-r_{k})\sum_{P}\pi_{k}(P)(\mathcal{P}-\mathrm{id}), so Γk​(rk)=1+2​(ϵk−rk)+𝒪⁡(ϵk​(ϵk−rk))\Gamma_{k}(r_{k})=1+2(\epsilon_{k}-r_{k})+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon_{k}(\epsilon_{k}-r_{k})). Taking logarithms and summing over the independent locations gives equation (43). The model–model term of the MMD multiplies two such weights, so its variance has a leading term of order Γ​(𝐫)2/N\Gamma(\mathbf{r})^{2}/N from fluctuations of one weight at a time and a term of order Γ​(𝐫)4/N2\Gamma(\mathbf{r})^{4}/N^{2} from both weights together

Capped allocation and the retained budget.

The capped profile in equation (27) solves the allocation step of problem (26) at a fixed total residual noise.

Lemma 4 (Capped allocation at a fixed budget).

Fix R∈[0,‖ϵ‖1]R\in[0,\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\right\rVert_{1}]. The unique solution of

min𝐫\displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{r}}\quad ‖𝐫‖2\displaystyle\left\lVert\mathbf{r}\right\rVert_{2}
subject to ‖𝐫‖1=R,0≤rk≤ϵk\displaystyle\left\lVert\mathbf{r}\right\rVert_{1}=R,\qquad 0\leq r_{k}\leq\epsilon_{k} (45)

is

rkcap​(R)=min⁡{ϵk,ν⁡(R)},r_{k}^{\mathrm{cap}}(R)=\min\{\epsilon_{k},\nu(R)\}, (46)

where ν⁡(R)≥0\nu(R)\geq 0 is chosen such that

∑k=1Lmin⁡{ϵk,ν⁡(R)}=R.\sum_{k=1}^{L}\min\{\epsilon_{k},\nu(R)\}=R. (47)

Proof sketch. The problem minimizes a strictly convex function over a polytope. Its Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions give rk=min⁡{ϵk,max⁡{0,ν}}r_{k}=\min\{\epsilon_{k},\max\{0,\nu\}\} for a multiplier ν\nu. Because ∑kmin⁡{ϵk,ν}\sum_{k}\min\{\epsilon_{k},\nu\} is continuous and nondecreasing in ν\nu, a value ν⁡(R)\nu(R) satisfying equation (47) exists, and strict convexity gives uniqueness.

It remains to choose the retained budget R⋆R^{\star} in equation (29). Let g⁡(R):=e−R​‖𝐫cap​(R)‖2g(R):=e^{-R}\left\lVert\mathbf{r}^{\mathrm{cap}}(R)\right\rVert_{2} denote the mismatch bound of the capped profile. Increasing RR raises only the capped entries, so dd​R​‖𝐫cap​(R)‖22=2​ν​(R)\frac{d}{dR}\left\lVert\mathbf{r}^{\mathrm{cap}}(R)\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=2\nu(R) and g′​(R)g^{\prime}(R) has the sign of ν⁡(R)−‖𝐫cap​(R)‖22\nu(R)-\left\lVert\mathbf{r}^{\mathrm{cap}}(R)\right\rVert_{2}^{2}. Since every entry is at most ν⁡(R)\nu(R), this quantity is at least ν​(R)​(1−R)\nu(R)(1-R), which is positive in the weak-noise regime R<1R<1. The mismatch bound therefore increases with RR, the feasible budgets form an interval, and R⋆R^{\star} is found by bisection. Algorithm 1 summarizes the procedure.

4.3 Budget-aware noise control

This subsection specifies the shot allocation and the validation estimator used by the GENIE controller, and then sketches the analysis behind Theorem 3 and Corollary 2.

Shot allocation and validation estimates.

Let Btr,tB_{\mathrm{tr},t} and Bpr,tB_{\mathrm{pr},t} denote the unspent training and probe budgets at step tt, initialized to (1−α)​B(1-\alpha)B and α​B\alpha B. Each training step receives an equal share of the remaining training budget, and each comparison an equal share of the remaining probe budget,

Nfuture,t:=Btr,tPcirc​(T−t),Nt:=⌊Nfuture,t⌋,Mt:=⌊Bpr,tJ​ut⌋,N_{\mathrm{future},t}:=\frac{B_{\mathrm{tr},t}}{P_{\mathrm{circ}}(T-t)},\qquad N_{t}:=\bigl\lfloor N_{\mathrm{future},t}\bigr\rfloor,\qquad M_{t}:=\Bigl\lfloor\frac{B_{\mathrm{pr},t}}{J\,u_{t}}\Bigr\rfloor, (48)

where utu_{t} is the number of comparisons remaining, including the current one. Subtracting the executions spent at each step keeps the policy within the budget of equation (30). At a comparison, the PER probes of candidate jj return independent outcome–weight pairs (Yt​j,a,Wt​j,a)(Y_{tj,a},W_{tj,a}) with |Wt​j,a|≤Γj|W_{tj,a}|\leq\Gamma_{j} and 𝔼⁡[Wt​j,a​κ​(Yt​j,a,⋅)]=μqθt𝐫(j)\mathbb{E}[W_{tj,a}\kappa(Y_{tj,a},\cdot)]=\mu_{q^{\mathbf{r}^{(j)}}_{\theta_{t}}}. On the validation sample 𝒮val={x1,…,xv}\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{val}}=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{v}\}, the controller uses the weighted U-statistic

L~val,tU​(j)=1v⁡(v−1)​∑i≠i′κ⁡(xi,xi′)+1Mt​(Mt−1)​∑a≠bWt​j,a​Wt​j,b​κ​(Yt​j,a,Yt​j,b)−2v​Mt∑i=1v∑a=1MtWt​j,aκ(xi,Yt​j,a),\begin{split}\widetilde{L}^{U}_{\mathrm{val},t}(j)={}&\frac{1}{v(v-1)}\sum_{i\neq i^{\prime}}\kappa(x_{i},x_{i^{\prime}})+\frac{1}{M_{t}(M_{t}-1)}\sum_{a\neq b}W_{tj,a}W_{tj,b}\,\kappa(Y_{tj,a},Y_{tj,b})\\ &-\frac{2}{vM_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{v}\sum_{a=1}^{M_{t}}W_{tj,a}\,\kappa(x_{i},Y_{tj,a}),\end{split} (49)

which, averaged over the fresh probes, recovers the validation U-statistic with exact generator expectations. Excluding the diagonal pairs removes the self-interaction bias, and the estimates are compared without clipping because a U-statistic can be negative. The standard error in the measurement radius is estimated conditionally on the validation data and accounts for the dependence among the pairwise terms. Algorithm 2 combines these rules with the selection rule (31).

Regret analysis.

The regret bound needs control over how fast candidate scores change between comparisons. On the circuit side, this is provided by the following sensitivity bound.

Lemma 5 (Risk sensitivity).

Suppose each of the dθ=dim(θ)d_{\theta}=\dim(\theta) parameters occurs once, through a Pauli rotation e−iθkPk/2e^{-i\theta_{k}P_{k}/2}, with fixed, parameter-independent CPTP noise channels and fixed measurement. Then, uniformly over admissible residual profiles,

|R𝐫​(θ)−R𝐫​(θ′)|≤LR​‖θ−θ′‖2,LR:=2​2​dθ.\left|R_{\mathbf{r}}(\theta)-R_{\mathbf{r}}(\theta^{\prime})\right|\leq L_{R}\|\theta-\theta^{\prime}\|_{2},\qquad L_{R}:=2\sqrt{2d_{\theta}}. (50)

Proof sketch. The parameter-shift rule writes each partial derivative of the kernel mean embedding μqθ𝐫\mu_{q^{\mathbf{r}}_{\theta}} as half the difference of the embeddings of two valid output distributions. Because every MMD is at most 2\sqrt{2}, each partial derivative of R𝐫R_{\mathbf{r}} is bounded by a constant, and summing over the dθd_{\theta} coordinates gives the bound.

Proof sketch of Theorem 3. Group the training steps by the comparison that governs them, and split the regret of each step into the selection error at that comparison and the change in scores since then. The selection error has three parts. The first is the probe error, which is controlled by the concentration of the weighted U-statistics with weights bounded by Γ¯\overline{\Gamma} and a union bound over the J​HJH estimates, and it gives the first term. The second is the measurement radius, which is at most 6​z​Γ¯2/Ms6z\overline{\Gamma}^{2}/\sqrt{M_{s}} because the standard error is bounded by the range of its per-shot terms, and it adds 6​z6z to the constant of the first term. The third is the validation error, which is controlled by av​(β)a_{v}(\beta) and by the distance δγ​Ds+2​εtol\delta_{\gamma}D_{s}+2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tol}} between candidate mean embeddings implied by equation (25), and it gives the second term. The change in scores within each block is bounded with Lemma 5 and Assumption 3 by summing the step sizes h/(t+1)h/(t+1), and together with the change of the budget penalty it gives the last term.

Proof sketch of Corollary 2. With B=Θ⁡(T)B=\Theta(T) and K=⌈T2/3⌉K=\lceil T^{2/3}\rceil, there are H=𝒪⁡(T1/3)H=\mathcal{O}(T^{1/3}) comparisons, so the first term of equation (34) is 𝒪~​(T2/3)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{2/3}). The second term is 𝒪~​(T/v)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T/\sqrt{v}) because Ds≤2D_{s}\leq\sqrt{2}. The last term is 𝒪⁡(T2/3​log⁡T)\mathcal{O}(T^{2/3}\log T) because Nfuture,0=(1−α)​B/(Pcirc​T)=Θ⁡(1)N_{\mathrm{future},0}=(1-\alpha)B/(P_{\mathrm{circ}}T)=\Theta(1).

4.4 Experimental Setup

We evaluate GENIE in simulation on three synthetic targets at n=12n=12 qubits and one real dataset (i.e., UCI Adult Census Becker and Kohavi (1996)), varying the training-set size, the hardware error rate and the execution budget. We first describe the setup for accessment on synthetic datasets first and spend the last paragraph on the real census experiment.

Synthetic Datasets.

The first is a binary blob distribution generated by eight prototype strings whose bits are flipped independently with probability 0.20.2. The second is a weighted fixed-cardinality distribution on the (126)=924\binom{12}{6}=924 strings of Hamming weight six, with weight parameter ω=6\omega=6. The third is the Boltzmann distribution of a ferromagnetic Ising ring at temperature 2.42.4. Their effective numbers of outcomes, eH⁡(p)e^{H(p)} with HH the Shannon entropy, are 16261626, 560560 and 13241324. In each run we draw m∈{64,256,1024,4096}m\in\{64,256,1024,4096\} samples from the target and hold out 20%20\% of them as the validation sample of the controller.

Model, loss and noise.

The Born machine is a hardware-efficient circuit with 1010 layers of single-qubit Pauli rotations and CNOT, giving 360360 parameters that each enter once through a Pauli rotation. Gradients are computed with the parameter-shift rule, so each update evaluates Pcirc=721P_{\mathrm{circ}}=721 circuits. The loss is the MMD U-statistic with the Gaussian mixture kernel on the Hamming distance, with bandwidths (0.5,1,2)×n/5(0.5,1,2)\times\sqrt{n/5}. Hardware noise consists of stochastic Pauli channels at the L=240L=240 noisy locations of the circuit, with per-location rates of mean ϵ¯∈{0.002,0.004,0.008}\bar{\epsilon}\in\{0.002,0.004,0.008\} shared by all runs. Simulations are implemented in JAX and run on CPUs.

Training, budgets and compared methods.

Each run performs T=500T=500 updates with the Adam optimizer at the starting learning rate of 0.10.1 which decays over time. Budgets are counted in circuit executions without any rescaling by the PER cost. The unit budget U=T​Pcirc×2000≈7.2×108U=T\,P_{\mathrm{circ}}\times 2000\approx 7.2\times 10^{8} corresponds to 20002000 shots per circuit at every step, and we consider B∈{1,5,25,125}×UB\in\{1,5,25,125\}\times U, with each step receiving an even share of the remaining budget as in equation (48). We compare four methods at the same budget. Three keep a fixed noise level throughout training, namely no mitigation (γ=γ¯\gamma=\bar{\gamma}), half mitigation (γ=γ¯/2\gamma=\bar{\gamma}/2) and full mitigation (γ=0\gamma=0). The fourth is GENIE, which compares the candidate levels γ/γ¯∈{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1}\gamma/\bar{\gamma}\in\{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1\} every K=25K=25 steps, starting at the first step, for 2020 comparisons per run. It uses z=1z=1, λ=1\lambda=1 and a probe fraction α=0.02\alpha=0.02, and its probe executions are charged to its own budget. These controller settings were tuned once at n=10n=10 and transferred unchanged.

Evaluation and statistics.

The grid comprises 33 targets, 33 error rates, 44 sample sizes and 44 budgets, giving 144144 conditions, each run with three seeds for a total of 17281728 runs. The figure of merit is the exact population loss LP=MMDκ2​(p,q)L_{P}=\mathrm{MMD}^{2}_{\kappa}(p,q) of the output distribution qq of the final model. Within each condition, we average LPL_{P} over the seeds and report the relative regret 100​(LP−L⋆)/L⋆100\,(L_{P}-L^{\star})/L^{\star}, where L⋆L^{\star} is the smallest seed-averaged loss among the four methods. Because this regret is bounded below and skewed, we report both its mean and its median.

Census experiment.

For the real-data experiment, we use the Adult census data Becker and Kohavi (1996). Its training split of 32,56132{,}561 people defines the target distribution pp, and its test split of 16,28116{,}281 people is used only to score the income questions. Each person is encoded in n=10n=10 bits, two Gray-coded bits each for age, education and weekly working hours, and one bit each for marital status, sex, a managerial or professional occupation, and income above 50K. The encoding was fixed before any training, and 845845 of its 10241024 strings occur in the data. The Born machine has 66 strongly entangling layers with 180180 parameters, so Pcirc=361P_{\mathrm{circ}}=361, and its L=120L=120 noisy locations have the mean error rate of 1.6%1.6\%. The kernel rule, the white-noise simulation, the T=500T=500 Adam updates and the controller settings follow the synthetic study, with a learning rate of max⁡{0.005, 0.1×0.5t/150}\max\{0.005,\,0.1\times 0.5^{t/150}\} at step tt. We draw m∈{64,128,256,512}m\in\{64,128,256,512\} people and hold out 20%20\% of them. The unit budget is U=T​Pcirc×2000≈3.6×108U=T\,P_{\mathrm{circ}}\times 2000\approx 3.6\times 10^{8} executions, and B∈{1,5,25,125,625}×UB\in\{1,5,25,125,625\}\times U. All scores are computed from the exact output distribution qq of the final model at the noise level at which it is deployed. The census shares compare the probability that qq assigns to an attribute with its share in pp.
